context_blurb:
Hold a magnet over a paper clip and the clip leaps up before anything touches it. Physicists explain such forces at a distance with fields: a field is the space around a charged object or a magnet where it pushes or pulls on other things. Fields steer every compass and hold some doors shut.

Every atom holds positive protons, locked in its centre, the nucleus, and light negative electrons, which move far more easily. Hair gives up electrons more easily than rubber, so rubbing a balloon on dry hair carries electrons off the hair and onto the balloon. The balloon turns negative and the hair, short of electrons, positive; no charge is made, and no proton moves.

Like charges, both positive or both negative, repel, and unlike charges attract, so balloon and hair cling. Rub two balloons on the same hair and hang them on threads, and they swing apart: both carry the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other away across the gap. More charge gives a harder push, and the push weakens as they spread apart.

A rubbed balloon even clings to a wall with no charge. The balloon's negative charge pushes the wall's like charges a little way back and draws the wall's opposite charges a little nearer, so the patch under the balloon turns slightly positive. Electric forces weaken with distance, so the nearer pull beats the farther push. On a metal door its extra electrons drain away, and it drops.

Magnets have their own rule: each has a north and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract. William Gilbert, an English doctor, studied them by experiment. He carved a lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, into a sphere, his terrella or little Earth. In 1581 the mariner Robert Norman had found that a compass needle free to tilt dips below level. Over Gilbert's ball such a needle lay level above the middle and dipped ever more steeply nearer a pole, until over the pole it pointed straight down. Since compasses dip that way across Earth, Gilbert argued in De Magnete, in 1600, that Earth itself is a giant magnet.

A compass needle's N end is its north-seeking pole, drawn toward the North Magnetic Pole in the Arctic. Since unlike poles attract, that pole must, by its kind, be a south pole: it is named for where it lies, not for what it is.

Earth is by far the stronger magnet, but its field at the surface is weak, and a magnet's field fades very fast with distance. So a few centimetres from a small bar magnet its field is many times Earth's, and a compass needle turns to face it; across the room its field falls far below Earth's, and the needle swings back to north.

Until 1820 no one had shown a link between electricity and magnetism. That April, lecturing in Copenhagen, Hans Christian Oersted sent a current through a wire over a compass needle that sat under glass. The needle turned aside from north, and when he broke the circuit it settled back. No current could reach the needle through the glass, so the current in the wire must have made a magnetic field, and that field turned the needle. Later tests showed the field runs in circles around the wire.

A coil of wire carrying a current is an electromagnet, a magnet made by electric current. Its strength grows with the current and with the number of turns, so winding more turns of the same wire onto a nail lets it lift more paper clips. From 1830 Joseph Henry wrapped his wire in silk so he could wind it layer on layer. An iron core matters most: it can make a coil thousands of times stronger than the coil alone.

An electromagnet is a magnet only while current flows. A magnetic lock grips a steel plate on a door with a force of some twelve hundred pounds, yet if the lock loses its power, the grip vanishes at once and the door comes free. Such a lock is called fail-safe: with no power, it traps no one in a fire. Many keep a standby battery for blackouts, but once the lock's own current stops, the door is free. A scrapyard crane drops its steel the same way.
